Queen Elizabeth II obituary

By: Laura Byrne | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We recognise the passing of an icon of the 20th century's and take a look at her legacy - both positive and complicated

Unique Selling Point:
Queen Elizabeth II was both the oldest and the longest-reigning monarch in British history when she passed away on Thursday 8 September 2022 at the age of 96. She had ruled for just over 70 years. It was a lifetime that spanned the Second World War, the first moon-landing, the birth of the internet and the dawn of the 21st century...and a reign that brought the monarchy firmly into the modern era.

Summary:
We take a brief look at the legacy of Queen Elizabeth II's reign, with historic moments from her coronation - the first to be televised - to the expansion of the Commonwealth and her ushering of the Royal Family into a new era of public attention and celebrity. We create a nuanced picture of the era she presided over, including the political end of colonialism and criticism that the Queen allowed Britain to blur over a bloody legacy.

Script:


[ST PAUL’S CATHEDRAL BELLS]
NEWS ANCHOR: This is BBC News from London. Buckingham Palace has announced the death of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II.
UPSOUND DIANA LUCAS: I would describe her as a true person, somebody who's got that backbone and stays true to her word.
UPSOUND HAMILTON WENDE: someone who did not present herself as a celebrity, she presented herself as something more, as a presence.
VOICEOVER: A life that spans a World War, the first moon-landing, the birth of the internet and the dawn of the 21st century is extraordinary indeed. Born Elizabeth Alexandra Mary Windsor in 1926, she acceded to the throne aged just 25 after the death of her father, King George VI in 1952.
UPSOUND ARLENE PRINSLOO: I think she brought stability to the monarchy.
VOICEOVER: Arlene Prinsloo is a journalist and royal enthusiast.
UPSOUND ARLENE PRINSLOO: She brought the monarchy into the modern age. If you think that her coronation was the first one to be to be televised. And I think for a lady of 96, she could adapt to the modern world. She was the first monarch to send a tweet.
VOICEOVER: Elizabeth was celebrated for her unwavering service, her dry sense of humour, and for making everyone feel at home.
UPSOUND: HAMILTON WENDE: She represents a kind of psychological symbol for British people and people perhaps in the Commonwealth of continuity, of tradition…
VOICEOVER: As a young journalist, Hamilton Wende had a brief encounter with Her Majesty on her 1995 visit to South Africa.
UPSOUND HAMILTON WENDE: She was moving through the crowd, greeting people, and she finally came to our little group. And then I said, you know, Your Majesty, I'm from South Africa. And she looked at me, and she said, you know, I do so love South Africa. And I was just about to say, Thank you, Your Majesty, when my German colleague interrupted and said, Yeah, Your Majesty, but you know, the crime here is just terrible. And she looked at him with these extraordinary blue eyes of hers. And there was a sort of a pause and she said, Well, you know, it must be so terribly difficult for young people these days. She responded with dignity and she responded in a very human way.
VOICEOVER: I personally experienced her poise and good humour first hand, albeit briefly and at a distance! In 1995, Carte Blanche producer Diana Lucas and I visited London to meet Britain’s so-called Royal Watchers.
CARTE BLANCHE ARCHIVE: ROYAL WATCHERS: If I knew where Charles was with Camilla at this very moment, I would be there, I promise you!
UPSOUND DEREK WATTS: The Queen had visited St Luke’s Hospital and was ambling past…
UPSOUND DIANA LUCAS: And there is an enormous crowd and we're right at the back. And so - desperation - I started having to push Derek forward.
UPSOUND DEREK WATTS: The British media are a strange lot. They’ll shout out at politicians, ministers, but the queen is sacred. And yet I’m with this producer who insists that I shout out at the Queen.
CARTE BLANCHE ARCHIVE: ROYAL WATCHERS: Derek: Ma’am! Carte Blanche South Africa. We’re looking forward to your visit to Namibia next month.
Queen: Oh, thank you very much.
Derek: Look forward to seeing you in a few weeks.
Queen: Thank you.
UPSOUND DEREK WATTS: She must have thought who’s this lout from somewhere in Southern Africa who’s not sticking to protocol, but she just, she handles the moment.
VOICEOVER: It may have been her dedication to good manners that enabled Elizabeth to navigate the Royal Family through a changing world, in which royals became celebrities whose scandals were fodder for the paparazzi and social media.
UPSOUND DIANA LUCAS: The rest of the royal family, they go up and down and there's sensational stories and blah, blah, blah. But the queen has just steadfastly followed her path and the path that she set for herself or that destiny set for her.
VOICEOVER: But that destiny is not universally celebrated.
UPSOUND CHRIS MAROLENG: Certainly mixed emotions, especially in Africa, about her death.
VOICEOVER: Chris Maroleng is the Executive Director of non-profit organisation Good Governance Africa.
UPSOUND CHRIS MAROLENG: Especially from younger generations, we've seen a very stark confrontation of this legacy of the British colonial empire.
VOICEOVER: Elizabeth was born into an Empire on which “the sun never set”. Through the 20th century, she presided over independence celebrations in one African country after another.
MNET ARCHIVE: THE QUEEN VISITS NAMIBIA (1991): QUEEN ELIZABETH: I ask you all to join me in a toast to the President of the Republic of Namibia [...] and to the happiness and prosperity of Namibia and its people.
But was she simply helping Britain gloss over its ugly colonial past?
UPSOUND CHRIS MAROLENG: People conflate, unfortunately, Queen Elizabeth II, the personality who has died, with the terrible legacy of the colonial experience. And I think it's important to distinguish, even though we are not trying to rebrand what was a bad experience of colonialism by and large for many Africans.
VOICEOVER: Elizabeth’s sense of duty was legendary and she rarely took a day off…in the very week of her death, she welcomed Liz Truss as Britain’s new Prime Minister.
UPSOUND ARLENE PRINSLOO: That whole work ethic, that she wanted to see this through. And she did. She was doing her job right up till the end.
VOICEOVER: With the passing of essentially the only reigning monarch of modern-day Britain, what is the future of the monarchy?
KING CHARLES III ADDRESS: ‘As the Queen herself did with such unswerving devotion, I too now solemnly pledge myself, throughout the remaining time God grants me, to uphold the constitutional principles at the heart of our nation.
VOICEOVER: Soon to be crowned King Charles the Third, at 73, Elizabeth’s heir is the oldest monarch ever to accede to the British throne.
UPSOUND ARLENE PRINSLOO: He's waited a long time to become a king. It's an internship of more than six decades.
UPSOUND CHRIS MAROLENG: I think we may see a very diminished role far removed from the direct role that Queen Elizabeth had with Africa as opposed to the contemporary experience that we could have of King Charles III.
VOICEOVER: It will take time before Charles is crowned… For now the British people remain in mourning and their late monarch will be laid to rest in a week’s time.
